profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an internal ML research proposal that extends a completed benchmark study on CNN architectures for accelerating unsteady CFD surrogates in virtual nuclear reactor digital twins. The team is reviewing whether the proposed follow-on design is ready to be approved for implementation in the RePIT framework. The proposal keeps the existing ConvLSTM-UNet baseline and adds a stabilization module for longer autoregressive rollouts on the small natural-convection dataset. Agenda: review whether the experimental design is sufficiently 'fair' relative to the prior paper, confirm what counts as the '10-step stability' target, check whether the RePIT integration plan is complete, and decide if the proposal can move from review into execution. Expected outcome: conditional approval of the design with a short list of revisions, although the two participants leave with subtly different beliefs about what exactly was approved.

members.name: Dr. Lena Hoffmann
members.expertise: Scientific machine learning, reduced-order modeling, benchmark design for physics-informed surrogate evaluation
members.background: Lena leads a national-lab collaboration on neural surrogates for thermal-hydraulic simulation and authored the previous RePIT benchmark comparing autoencoder, UNet, and ConvLSTM-UNet models on small-data natural convection sequences.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved quickly so the team can reuse the prior benchmark infrastructure and submit a workshop paper within the quarter, but she is concerned that changing too many evaluation details will make results harder to compare against the earlier benchmark.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the extension should be 'fair,' it means preserving the same train/validation/test split, same normalization pipeline, and same rollout protocol used in the earlier benchmark so longitudinal comparison remains clean.

The '10-step stability' target refers to maintaining acceptable rollout behavior over 10 autoregressive predictions after the first predicted frame, consistent with how the prior study discussed reliability limits.

Integrating the design into 'RePIT' mainly means plugging the new stabilization module into the existing research evaluation pipeline and logging format, not hardening the code for the reactor digital-twin deployment stack.
The 'baseline checkpoint' everyone references is the best ConvLSTM-UNet model from the final benchmark table trained on the canonical natural-convection split from the published study.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.role: Senior Research Engineer for Simulation ML Systems
members.expertise: ML systems for scientific computing, reproducible experiment pipelines, deployment-facing benchmarking for CFD surrogate models
members.background: Arjun maintains the RePIT codebase and adapts research models into reusable components for downstream digital-twin prototypes used by reactor simulation teams.
members.private_state: He wants the proposal to produce implementation-ready artifacts that can transfer into a broader digital-twin workflow, and he is worried the current design review will approve something that is only publication-ready rather than operationally reproducible.
hidden_assumptions: When the design is described as 'fair,' it means equalized tuning and compute budget across all compared variants in the new study, even if some preprocessing or split details differ from the earlier paper.
The '10-step stability' target refers to 10 future timesteps beyond the last available context frame in a full closed-loop rollout, because that is how downstream users interpret prediction horizon.
Integrating into 'RePIT' includes containerized training, inference hooks, and config compatibility with the digital-twin prototype branch, not just the internal benchmark scripts.

The 'baseline checkpoint' refers to the latest cleaned ConvLSTM-UNet weights retrained after a bugfix in the data loader on the maintained main branch, since those are the default assets in the current repository.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a fair comparison
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the revised design must remain a 'fair comparison' with the prior CNN benchmark.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means fairness as methodological continuity with the published benchmark: same canonical split, same normalization choices, and same rollout setup so the new stabilization module can be compared cleanly against prior results.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means fairness as resource parity in the new review: each model variant gets the same tuning budget, wall-clock budget, and implementation quality, even if some data handling details are updated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research, 'fair comparison' is a highly shared positive phrase that usually goes unquestioned; both participants hear it as obviously correct and assume the other is invoking the same standard.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the proposal should demonstrate 'stable predictions for about 10 timesteps.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the model should avoid visibly unacceptable drift for 10 autoregressive updates after seeding from the initial truth window, matching the prior paper's practical reliability framing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the model must satisfy the acceptance threshold at the 10th forecasted future frame in a fully closed-loop horizon counted from the end of context, as a deployment-facing criterion.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both understand the phrase as echoing the seed paper, and neither expects horizon counting conventions to differ because the number '10' sounds precise enough to imply shared interpretation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the design should be 'integrated into RePIT' before execution starts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes only the experiment runner, result logging schema, and benchmark notebook support needed for internal comparison.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes those items plus container definitions, config interfaces, and hooks required by the digital-twin prototype branch so the artifact is reusable outside the benchmark sandbox.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: RePIT is both a research framework and an engineering codebase, so saying 'integrated' sounds sufficiently concrete while hiding different assumptions about which subparts are in scope.

misalignment_points.topic: Which baseline checkpoint is being reused
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to reusing 'the existing ConvLSTM-UNet baseline checkpoint' to save time.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the exact published benchmark checkpoint associated with the canonical split and figures from the previous study.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the newer repository-default checkpoint retrained after the data-loader fix, which is operationally the maintained baseline asset.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one baseline model family under discussion and both checkpoints are informally called 'the ConvLSTM-UNet baseline,' so the reference feels unambiguous unless someone explicitly cites a run ID.

When I say reuse the existing ConvLSTM-UNet baseline checkpoint, I mean the exact published benchmark model on the canonical split, because otherwise the comparison to the old tables starts to drift.
